articles.title: Western Michigan beats Monmouth 49-14 as 5 key errors cause blowout
articles.summary: Monmouth lost 49-14 to Western Michigan on Saturday night in Kalamazoo. It was the first game after the Broncos' controversial loss to Michigan.
articles.body:
There may not be moral victories in college football, but there is progress.

Monmouth football went on the road against the momentary darling of the sport and a Mid-American Conference powerhouse. The final score will look predictable on paper. The Hawks lost 49-14 to Western Michigan on Saturday night in Kalamazoo. It was the first game after the Broncos ' controversial loss to Michigan had galvanized college football fans across the country in support, and WMU head coach Lance Taylor had foreshadowed the team's response after that painful finish.

"Hey, don't feel sorry for us," Taylor told reporters after the Michigan game. "Feel sorry for the teams that we're going to play."

But don't feel sorry for Monmouth, either. Overall, the Hawks (1-2) put together their best performance of the season as they went toe-to-toe with the Broncos (1-1) in the first half in particular. A much smaller percentage of Monmouth's plays were fatal self-inflicted wounds, and it was enough to obfuscate the team's considerable progress in the third game of the season.

"We did some things well. We moved the ball well, we got stops, but it's putting it all together," Monmouth head coach Jeff Gallo said. "That's a good team, but we're out here trying to compete to win and we can play better. We'll keep pushing to play better."

In terms of yards, Monmouth out-gained Western Michigan at a rate of 431 yards to 414. They had 26 first downs compared to 24 for the Broncos. They converted third downs at a superior rate, going 11-for-20 compared to 4-for-9 for WMU. But of course, the many positives were disconnected and out of sync.

A handful of lapses tell the story. Two lost fumbles at critical junctures. Consecutive drops that derailed the team's first promising drive. One disastrous instance of lacking punt coverage. And a dose of bad luck that was not Monmouth's fault, as a tremendous early interception was called back because of a dubious pass interference call.

"We had a pick in the first half they took off the board with the pass interference call," Gallo said. "I thought we did a good job trying to contain the quarterback and the running back. And in the same half, they hit some big plays over our head, but we had guys there to contest. You have to keep competing for the ball in the air."

As painful as it is to process the mistakes, that shouldn't blur the portrait of the team's progress. Monmouth's defense, when not facing drives that started in their own territory, was sharp against the high-powered rushing offense of a potential College Football Playoff contender from the Group of 6. The Hawk offense is increasingly finding winning concepts and plays that suit the strengths of their playmakers, and the depth was on display as the were able to move the football in a variety of ways.

"We have to play complimentary football, meaning getting a stop and a score. It's putting it all together," Gallo said. "Through the course of the whole game. Not a quarter, not a half, not a drive. It's playing a full game as a team."

The mistakes were disastrous, but the team's response was inspired. The errors didn't snowball like they did in the season opener against Tennessee Tech . In particular after the second lost fumble, the Monmouth defense made a tremendous stand to force a punt. The individual flashes of brilliance were numerous, and the collective groups on the offensive line and front seven are increasingly looking like they can be upper echelon units in the CAA.

Monmouth held WMU star running back Jalen Buckley to just 28 yards on 10 carries, although he had three goal line touchdowns. But the commitment to defending the run came at a cost, as Broncos quarterback Broc Lowry was 14-for-20 for 212 yards with three passing touchdowns and added another 40 rushing yards.

"We did a good job stopping their inside run game. Most of their stuff came on the wider speed sweep or option stuff," Gallo said. "If you want to win, you've got to win the line of scrimmage."

Monmouth will have to prove that the improvement is authentic next Saturday against Albany, a team that was the Hawks' kryptonite at the end of last season that kept them out of the FCS playoffs. This year's Great Danes team has seen a prompt return to contender status with wins by multiple scores over New Hampshire and Long Island plus a near-upset of MAC member Buffalo.

That matchup will be the true barometer of where the Hawks stand, coming at crucial juncture at the one-third mark of the regular season. But Monmouth is moving in the right direction, even if it doesn't feel that way after the final score on Saturday night.

"There's things to build off of. We've got to keep improving as we get into conference play," Gallo said. "The outcome is the outcome. We're gonna learn how to grow."

Monmouth U football wins season opener against Sacred Heart U 31-24

After Monmouth only trailed 7-0 late in the first quarter, the team's upset hopes were still very much alive. But the second quarter marked the start of the Hawks' errors. After solid success moving the football, their first promising drive reached the Western Michigan 30-yard line. Then consecutive drops by Greg Genross and Keshawn Mister led to a turnover on downs.

Those mistakes were amplified just over a minute later when Monmouth cornerback Omar Ibrahim made a spectacular diving interception, but it was called back because of pass interference. The Broncos went on to finish the drive with their second touchdown.

Later in the second quarter after the teams traded three-and-outs, Monmouth had a costly special teams mistake that echoed the season opener against Tennessee Tech. Lackadaisical punt coverage led to a 76-yard return by WMU's Kordell Gouldsby that set up the Broncos at the Hawks' 5-yard line. They promptly punched in the touchdown to make it 21-0.

The Monmouth offense again rallied to put together another long drive, potentially scoring before the half to regain momentum. But at the WMU 5-yard, the Hawks ran a jet sweep motion and there was a mistake with the mesh point on the handoff as the play was a run to Kenny Smith . He ran into the motion man and fumbled the ball in the ultimate self-inflicted wound.

The final lapse was lesser by comparison, but it was the final nail in the coffin. The resilient Hawks got their first touchdown on their first possession of the second half. Clinging to hope while trailing 35-7, they were piecing together another scoring drive but faced a 4th-and-3 in their own territory. Smith was wide open in the flat for the first down, but yet another drop led to a turnover on downs.

Individually, there were more than a few positive takeaways for the Hawks. Beginning at the end, Keyport native Nazir Treadwell got his first career touchdown on a goal line run with 15 seconds left in the game. More broadly, his involvement brings an added dimension to the Monmouth running game.

To be clear, Smith and Jennings are quality backs and performed very well against the WMU defense, combining for 200 yards of total offense. But their skillsets are duplicative, whereas the 6-1 and 225-pound Treadwell brings a change of pace with his power. He also showed he can be serviceable as a receiver with 10-yard reception.

Those collective positives from the stable of running backs are also a testament to the continued growth of the offensive line. The Hawks kept experimenting with different combinations, but Penn State transfer Brady O'Hara has emerged as a formidable force at tackle and Lafayette transfer Reed Collins had several strong moments at the point of attack in the run game. The pass protection was also solid against the tough WMU front.

That stability in protection allowed Frankie Weaver to see a lot more growth in his third game of the season. He was 28-for-46 for 273 yards and a touchdown, and should have had even more production if not for the drops. He looked more comfortable delivering the ball on intermediate routes and found eight different receivers over the course of the evening.

None of those targets were more impactful than Tra Neal, who turned in a star showing against Western Michigan. He finished with seven catches for 106 yards and a touchdown, and almost singlehandedly put the Hawks on the board with a huge run after catch on a 44-yard gain that set up his own 5-yard touchdown reception.

And lastly, the defensive front seven continues to look like a unit that can stifle CAA offenses. The pass rush left a little to be desired, but the ability to be tougher than WMU on the interior against the run was astounding. Defending the sweeps and outside runs was an issue, and so angles and pursuit might need to be a continued point of emphasis. But the general motor and ability to rally to the football was impressive. Ryan Russo was the star of the group, finishing with 10 tackles and a sack.

articles.title: Why Lane Kiffin said LSU's struggles before Ole Miss game might be good timing
articles.summary: Lane Kiffin wasn't happy LSU struggled vs La Tech but with Ole Miss up next, he said it could work in the Tigers' favor.
articles.body:
No. 8 LSU beat Louisiana Tech 45-14 on Sept. 12, but the Tigers led just 10-7 at halftime. LSU quarterback Sam Leavitt threw three interceptions in the game a week after the 51-10 rout of Clemson.

LSU coach Lane Kiffin said because the No. 8 Tigers (2-0) face No. 11 Ole Miss (2-0) on the road next on Sept. 19 (6:30 p.m., ABC), it might not have been such a bad thing that they struggled some vs Louisiana Tech.

"It was good because of that," Kiffin said of facing Ole Miss next. "We're getting ready to go on the road in the SEC vs a really good team that has played really well for years at that place.

"It was good because it's hard to get their (LSU's) attention after last week ... I'm glad it happened."

Lane Kiffin, LSU football coach returning to Ole Miss for Week 3 game

Ole Miss coach Pete Golding and the Rebels will go up against Kiffin less than one year after Kiffin left before the College Football Playoff.

Why Lane Kiffin's return to Ole Miss as LSU coach is such a big deal

Kiffin left Ole Miss on Nov. 30, taking the LSU job before the Rebels played in the College Football Playoff for the first time.

Kiffin lobbied to coach Ole Miss during the CFP but Rebels AD Keith Carter said that wasn't an option once Kiffin left.

Ole Miss promoted Pete Golding to head coach from defensive coordinator on the day Kiffin left for LSU.

Golding led Ole Miss to CFP wins over Tulane and Georgia. The Rebels season ended in the CFP semifinals with a loss to Miami.

Sam Hutchens covers Ole Miss for the Clarion Ledger. Email him at Shutchens@gannett.com or reach him on X at @Sam_Hutchens_

articles.title: UTSA, McCown shed years of burden with late win over rival Texas State
articles.summary: The Roadrunners found redemption after two straight losses to the Bobcats, hitting back after two years of slow starts and road woes.
articles.body:
SAN MARCOS - As UTSA quarterback Owen McCown was preparing for his final season, he felt a lingering weight on his shoulders.

He carried the burden of two straight losses to rival Texas State, of slow starts and road woes and missed opportunities in close losses. No matter what drills or exercises the Roadrunners devised, he knew he couldn't replicate those moments. He dove into the mental aspect as much as he could, searching for answers that might pay off when the situation finally arrived.

With UTSA trailing in the final two minutes against Texas State in a pivotal early season showdown Saturday in San Marcos, McCown delivered. The Roadrunners orchestrated a drive that ended in a 25-yard touchdown run by Brandon High with 14 seconds remaining, providing the final blow in a 30-26 win over the Bobcats.

"Obviously that's something we've been working on, and it showed today," McCown said. "To go out my last year against a rival here, a road win on a two-minute drill, it's big time. It says a lot about our team."

UTSA coach Jeff Traylor felt the same weight McCown did, and he had worked since January to try to alleviate it. From the "painful" decisions to make changes to his staff, reaching as high up as new offensive coordinator Rick Bowie, to a renewed focus on identity and UTSA's Triangle of Toughness culture.

The roster was built with players who offered maturity and experience rather than raw talent, and Traylor worked to help the group jell. The team's mantra this year is Ubuntu, an African philosophy meaning "I am because we are."

"This was a group that was made to win in that environment," Traylor said. "This group is wired for that."

Traylor said part of the mindset he worked to instill was being prepared and proactive in every situation, and the Roadrunners put that in action as they battled the elements Saturday.

With temperatures pushing 100 degrees, UTSA rented six cooling benches that were chilled to provide relief from head to toe. The benches were covered with sun shades and surrounded by misters, and the Roadrunners had additional misting fans that could be worn as backpacks.

Even in the locker room, the Roadrunners used portable air conditioning units connected to the ceiling vents, with extra fans to help that cool air circulate.

UTSA also dealt with electrical issues on the sideline that sometimes knocked out communication. Instead, McCown jogged to the coaches or relied on hand signals for play calls, just as the Roadrunners trained when they drilled similar situations in practice.

Traylor stressed that credit for the win was owed to all levels of the program, naming off members of the team's equipment, training and operations staffs. He also thanked UTSA's administration for spending to make everything possible.

"There was so much forward thinking put in this game, and our kids just kept playing," Traylor said. "It was a great win. Great win."

Another part of that planning for Traylor this week involved heaping praise on Texas State at every opportunity. After the Bobcats had won the past two in the series, Traylor said he "wanted them to feel that they had the weight and were supposed to win, that the torch had been passed."

He knew Texas State had established a reputation as a burgeoning program, and he heard from fans who were upset to see Bobcats ads at the airport, or on the front page of the Express-News on the Sunday entering rivalry week.

The competition for talent, resources and prestige between the two programs is far from settled, but at least on Saturday, the Roadrunners were glad to be celebrating a win.

"I was proud for my fans. That's two years they had to listen to that stuff," Traylor said. "That trophy had been in that spot in my office, and we ain't put a damn thing in that spot in two years. There's a nice little warm place for that thing when it gets back home."

Texas State led 17-7 at halftime before UTSA rallied, taking a 24-23 lead on an A'Marion Peterson touchdown run with about 12 minutes to play. After the Bobcats converted a chip shot field goal with less than five minutes to play, McCown said he took the field thinking, "Go win the game."

He converted a fourth-and-5 with a pass to David Amador, then delivered on another fourth-and-5 when he kept the ball on a run-pass option play and extended just beyond the line to gain.

The Roadrunners converted five of six attempts on fourth down, as Traylor felt confident putting the game in McCown's hands. Traylor said he's never "seen him so determined" or lead as forcefully as he did through this week's practices.

"I wasn't going home without letting him have chances," Traylor said. "I know everybody's looking at me crooked, but I was going down with him."

After four more short completions, the Roadrunners were in field goal range with less than 30 seconds to play, seemingly content to settle for a winning kick in the closing seconds.

But running back Brandon High ended the game in more emphatic fashion, rumbling around the right side of the line for a 25-yard score.

"The previous play, we kind of ran the same play, so I knew it was going to be there," High said. "When I seen the gap, I just took it."

High said the payoff was a moment two years in the making, as he entered Saturday still motivated by a 49-10 loss to the Bobcats the last time the Roadrunners visited San Marcos. UTSA now holds a 6-2 lead in the rivalry series.

The Roadrunners exorcised a few other demons on Saturday, finding a road win after going 3-10 away from the Alamodome the past two years. Following a 3-4 start in 2025 and a 2-4 mark to open 2024, the Roadrunners are 2-0 for the first time since 2021.

"It gives us a ton of momentum. Kind of lifts that road-game, two-minute-drill persona off our back a little bit," McCown said.

"For this to happen the way it did is super special."
